items.q: The better question to ask about a task is:
options: Can an assistant do this?
How often do I do it, and what does it cost me to check?
Is this task important?
items.explain: "Can it?" is almost always a qualified yes, which tells you nothing about whether you should. Frequency and verification cost do.

items.q: Verification cost is:
options: The monthly price of the assistant
The time it takes you to confirm the output is right
How long the assistant takes to respond
items.explain: If checking takes as long as doing the task, you have moved the work rather than reduced it.

items.q: Which task sits in the box where the real gains are?
options: A rare task where a mistake would be costly
A frequent task whose output you can check at a glance
A task you have never done before
items.explain: Frequent and cheap to check repays the setup. Rare tasks do not, and unverifiable ones transfer risk instead of saving time.

items.q: Asking for a "professional tone" tends to produce generic email because:
options: The model cannot process tone instructions
An adjective selects the average of all business email it has seen
Professional email is inherently formulaic
items.explain: Supplying two of your own sent emails gives it specific evidence to match, instead of an average to reach for.

items.q: Which email should you always write yourself?
options: Confirming a meeting time
An apology
Forwarding a document with a one-line note
items.explain: An apology you did not compose is not one. Where the effort is the message, delegating it removes the message.

items.q: A drafted email contains a deadline you never agreed to and you send it. This is:
options: Your responsibility — it went out in your name
A vendor defect
Not a problem unless the recipient objects
items.explain: Sending is the act that makes it yours, which is why every name, number and commitment is read before it goes.

items.q: The safest use of a summary of a document you have not read is:
options: As a map to decide which sections to read properly
As a replacement, provided the summary is detailed
As material to quote in your own work
items.explain: Repeating a summary's claims as your own knowledge asserts things you have not checked, in a form that sounds like you did.

items.q: Asking a summary to quote the source helps because:
options: Quoting makes models more accurate
A quote is checkable, and paraphrase is where a hedge disappears
Quotes make the summary more complete
items.explain: You can search the document for a quote. "May reduce costs in some settings" becoming "reduces costs" is exactly what a quote exposes.

items.q: Summaries systematically lose:
options: The central argument
Hedging, conditions and dissent
Dates and figures
items.explain: Summarising optimises for the main thrust, and qualifiers are not the main thrust — though in contracts and papers they are often the point.

items.q: An answer carrying four citations means:
options: Four sources independently confirmed it
Four pages were retrieved and used while composing it
The claim has been fact-checked
items.explain: Citation records retrieval, not verification. The page may not contain the specific claim assembled around it.

items.q: The fastest way to catch a citation that does not support its claim:
options: Count the citations
Search the linked page for the specific number or phrase
Ask the assistant how confident it is
items.explain: Searching for the exact claim rather than the topic is where most failures surface. A model's stated confidence is not evidence.

items.q: Why ask for the strongest evidence against a claim?
options: Negative questions produce shorter answers
A question with the answer baked in retrieves agreeable material
It makes the assistant search more sources
items.explain: Supporting material exists for almost any position. Permitting a no, and permitting "the evidence is mixed", is what surfaces disagreement.

items.q: In a structured meeting summary, the most valuable section is usually:
options: Decisions
The unclear and unresolved items
Attendees
items.explain: Decisions you already know. What nobody settled, and what has no owner, is the follow-up list a tidy summary hides.

items.q: A tidy meeting summary can be worse than messy notes because:
options: It takes longer to read
Its cleanliness implies an agreement the meeting never reached
It leaves out the date
items.explain: Readable prose resolves ambiguity, producing a written record of a decision nobody made — which later becomes the authority.

items.q: Before transcribing a meeting you should:
options: Confirm everyone present knows and agrees
Nothing — it is a standard tool feature
Mention it when you circulate the notes
items.explain: In many jurisdictions consent is a legal requirement rather than a courtesy, and automatic transcription counts.

items.q: In planning, assistants are genuinely reliable at:
options: Estimating durations
Listing steps and dependencies you have forgotten
Deciding which milestones matter
items.explain: Decomposition draws on many descriptions of how work gets done. Durations and priorities depend on your situation, which it cannot see.

items.q: AI time estimates lean optimistic because:
options: Models are tuned to be encouraging
Written accounts describe the intended path more than the delayed one
They assume you work on nothing else
items.explain: The estimate reflects how long tasks are described as taking, and descriptions skew towards the plan rather than the waiting.

items.q: A pre-mortem asks the assistant to:
options: List general risks
Assume the plan failed and give specific likely reasons
Estimate each phase
items.explain: Assuming failure and demanding specifics surfaces preventable problems. "Poor communication" is not a reason you can act on.

items.q: A new routine should be sized so that:
options: It fills the time you have on a good day
You can complete it on your worst realistic day
It covers every task you identified
items.explain: A routine is tested in the week you are ill and behind. One abandoned in week two saves nothing and cost you the setup.

items.q: The paste test asks whether:
options: The assistant offers an enterprise tier
You would be comfortable if this text appeared in an email outside your organisation
The text fits in the context window
items.explain: It is a fast proxy for confidentiality that works without reading a policy. If the answer is no, the text does not go in.

items.q: An enterprise tier usually means:
options: Your input is guaranteed private
Your text is not used for training, which is a narrower promise
Your text is never stored at all
items.explain: Not used for training says nothing about storage, processing location, or the obligations you personally are under.

items.q: Decisions about people should stay with a human because:
options: The output is usually obviously poor
Accountability cannot move to a tool, and the person is owed a human judgement
Models are slower at these decisions
items.explain: The output often reads well, which is the danger. Someone must be answerable, and being sorted by something that cannot be argued with is its own harm.

items.q: "The difficulty is the point" describes work where:
options: The task is unusually technical
The effort is the product — thinking it through is how you understand it
The deadline is tight
items.explain: Hand it over and you get the artefact without the understanding it was for, which is invisible now and expensive when you must defend it.
